business.overview:
GE Aerospace is the world's largest jet engine manufacturer, spun off from General Electric in April 2024 as a pure-play aerospace company. The company supplies engines for both commercial aviation (LEAP for 737 MAX/A320neo, GE9X for 777X, GEnx) and defense/propulsion (F110, T700 for military applications).

The business benefits from a massive installed base of 44,000+ engines generating recurring aftermarket revenue that accounts for over 60% of total revenue. Post-COVID aviation recovery combined with defense spending tailwinds create a dual growth engine. Revenue split is approximately 70% commercial aviation and 30% defense/propulsion technologies.

risks.riskSummary: Outstanding business quality with dominant market position, but current entry carries elevated risk due to extreme valuation (42x FPE, 8.55 PEG), overbought technicals (RSI 73), and 8.5% extension from EMA20.

riskCards.title: Valuation Risk
points: Forward PE 42x and PEG 8.55 price in years of flawless growth
P/B 21x and EV/EBITDA 34.7x leave no margin of safety
Any earnings miss would trigger a sharp de-rating
riskCards.verdict: Premium valuation justified by quality but leaves no room for execution stumbles

riskCards.title: Supply Chain & Production Constraints
points: Engine production still constrained by supply chain bottlenecks
Boeing delivery issues impact LEAP engine shipment pace
Aftermarket demand partially masks new engine production headwinds
riskCards.verdict: Recurring aftermarket revenue (60%+) cushions production-related shortfalls

riskCards.title: Geopolitical — Turkey Engine Sale
points: Congressional opposition to planned engine sale to Turkey
Could set precedent restricting future defense export deals
riskCards.verdict: Manageable — defense is ~30% of revenue and Turkey is one of many export markets

riskCards.title: Cyclical Aviation Exposure

Recession would reduce airline capex and engine orders
Aftermarket may slow if airlines defer maintenance spending
riskCards.verdict: Installed base of 44,000+ engines ensures baseline maintenance demand even in downturns
